summary: SwarmResearch is an orchestrator-subagent harness, packaged as three Claude Code skills, in which a Shepherd agent holds summaries of all attempts and spawns Explorer (fresh context) or Optimizer (forked context) Search agents, each working on its own git branch. On 15 open-ended optimization tasks (math, ADRS systems, ALE-Bench-Lite heuristics) it is compared with EvoX and CORAL under a $50 budget, plus a fixed-scaling study and a speculative-decoding case study.

claims.claim: Better or comparable to SOTA LLM-guided evolution and multi-agent techniques on 13/15 tasks
claims.evidence: Table 1, single run per method per task with Opus 4.6. Text is internally inconsistent: §3.2 says SwarmResearch strictly exceeds CORAL on 10/15 and matches 2, while the takeaway box says exceeds on 8 and similar on 5. Several 'wins' are tiny (Circle Packing 2.635996 vs CORAL 2.635985). EvoX underperforms its own paper because it was run with Opus instead of GPT-5; reproduced CORAL is worse than its published numbers.

claims.claim: SwarmResearch makes larger, higher-level code changes (1.7x-3.2x lines changed)
claims.evidence: §3.3 / Fig. 5: median of per-task mean lines changed; lines changed is a proxy for 'higher-level exploration', and EvoX diffs are measured only on improving programs.

claims.claim: Orchestrator-guided scaling beats optimal fixed serial/parallel scaling
claims.evidence: Table 2: 4/5 tasks (2/3 math, 2/2 systems) using Minimax-M2.5 in a minimal Pi harness; 5 tasks only, single runs; orchestrator adds 7.7% output tokens.

§4: 100 held-out tasks, 5 seeds; accuracy drops from 65.8% to 60.6%. Gain mostly from batching, which existing inference engines already implement; novel ideas 'performed poorly' and one claimed improvement was 'unsubstantiated' on re-evaluation.

patterns.note: Each search agent works on its own git branch/worktree; shared git history beat independent agents in fixed scaling (§3.4). Evidence is single-run.
Fresh-context Explorer subagents reduce anchoring; weakly supported by diff-size proxy and Table 1.
Shepherd orchestrator helps on scaling study, but §3.5 says its steering is near-greedy and it struggles to plan strategically even with heavy prompting.
Harness shipped as skills for Claude Code.
Two-tier context (summaries to orchestrator, local context to workers) is the core hypothesis; not ablated separately.
Fixed $50/task budgets; full benchmark run cost about $1,700 (App. B).

methodology.sample: 15 open-ended optimization tasks (5 math, ADRS systems tasks, 5 ALE-Bench-Lite heuristics); 5 tasks for scaling study; 1 case study
methodology.baselines: EvoX and CORAL via public implementations; both ran worse than their published results in authors' hands (EvoX with non-native model)
methodology.models: Claude Opus 4.6 via Claude Code for main comparison; Minimax-M2.5 for scaling study
methodology.variance: Single run per method per task (App. B argues multiple runs are too costly); 5 seeds only in the case-study evaluation
methodology.ablations: Minimal-harness scaling study isolates orchestrator; no ablation of Explorer vs Optimizer or two-tier context
methodology.contamination_controls: Open-ended tasks with evaluator-only API access; no internet
methodology.languages: Task programs mostly Python/C++-style optimization code; not stated as multi-language evaluation

standards.artifacts: Code at github.com/SwarmResearch/SwarmResearch; skill prompts in Appendix C

biases.detail: One run per method per task on stochastic high-temperature search; authors acknowledge estimates are unstable.
EvoX run with Opus although it performs better with GPT models; reproduced CORAL below its published results.
Lines of code changed used as evidence of 'higher-level exploration'.
CORAL win counts differ between §3.2 (10 exceed/2 match) and the RQ takeaway (8 exceed/5 similar).
Main comparison only with Opus 4.6; scaling study only Minimax-M2.5.
Open-ended optimization with scalar evaluators, not feature development or maintenance in real codebases.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Claude Code / Opus 4.6 used as runtime, not evaluated as a product
coi.detail: Academic authors evaluating their own system against reproduced competitors; self-evaluation but no commercial conflict.

verdict_reason: Interesting harness design (branch-per-subagent, fresh-context explorers, summary-only orchestrator) with released code, but single-run comparisons, weakened baselines, internally inconsistent win counts and tiny margins mean the 13/15 headline is not reliable. Admit as design evidence for parallel branch isolation, not as proof of superiority.
applicability: Weak transfer: tasks are scalar-scored optimization problems, not Java services or delivery features. Two ideas are portable to a mixed-host harness: run parallel agents in separate git branches/worktrees and pass only short attempt summaries upward, so no single context accumulates everything; and budget each run with a hard $ cap. For the team's several repositories, branch isolation per agent is consistent with the AGENTS.md rule that two mutating agents must not share one tree. The paper's own §4 warning that agents produce plausible-but-wrong claims needing expensive human review argues for deterministic verifiers (Maven/Gradle tests, contract tests) rather than orchestrator judgment. Skills are Claude-Code-specific packaging, so port the pattern, not the implementation.
